versions.body:
# Secret Timing and Root Directory Proposal

This page preserves a proposal from the time to handle two interface issues together. It never became a settled implementation guide. It remains here because someone did follow this line of reasoning during review and investigate further. Looking back, the two issues were similar only in that “both occurred near the creation path”; their dependency relationship was unclear.

The initial idea was straightforward: as soon as the Secret creation call returned, treat the version as ready for the next step; in the same round, pass the nested directory containing the application into the Backend creation request. The former aimed to eliminate waiting, while the latter aimed to avoid requiring callers to use separate entry points for different repository layouts. The draft did not distinguish between “the request has been accepted” and “the version can now be read by downstream services”. Nor did it explain where the directory value came from or whether an empty value was equivalent to the repository root directory. These were the main reasons this proposal was later abandoned.

## The Retained Old Proposal

The old proposal described version timing as a short chain: create the Secret, obtain the returned object, and continue with authorization and subsequent configuration. Here, “return” was treated as a completion signal, rather than merely providing an operation handle. The benefit was a short call path, with failures also confined to a single command; the cost was that, with asynchronous operations, errors would be attributed to the authorization or configuration stage even though the actual stopping point might be earlier.

At the time, no dedicated waiting logic was proposed. This was not because the absence of timing issues had been confirmed, but because of concern that putting polling at the command layer would turn failure information about the original Secret operation into a waiting error that was hard to explain. This reasoning focused too much on the length of the interaction and did not supply the missing assessment of version state, so it can no longer serve as a basis for implementation.

The other half of the old proposal held that the root directory did not need a separate parameter contract: default repository layouts would continue through the original creation path, and a nested application directory would only be passed along on an attempted basis when the caller already had one. “Attempted” was not clearly defined here. It could mean that the request contained a value, or merely that a local path was involved in preparation; these two cases have different implications for locating the codebase after creation.

The old draft also assumed that the two changes could be rolled back together: if either issue arose, restoring the original creation call would suffice. This assumption was also too optimistic. Waiting for a Secret version and the repository directory field belong to different boundaries: the former affects when subsequent access begins, while the latter affects which application directory the creation request describes. Giving them a shared rollback action would only make it unclear during troubleshooting which change caused the difference.

## Code Adjacency Observed at the Time

The investigation started at `src/functions/secrets.ts`. The file header imports `../utils`, `../operation-poller`, `../gcp/cloudfunctions`, and `../gcp/cloudfunctionsv2` together. This adjacency once encouraged the interpretation of the version issue as “polling infrastructure already exists; we can just wire it up later”. But these imports alone cannot determine whether polling should cover Secret creation, the authorization action, or another asynchronous operation; the old proposal treated this gap as an implementation detail that could be omitted by default.

Directory pass-through did not have equally direct clues in this entry-point record. Early discussions grouped it with Secret more to meet the same GA closeout than because the two shared a function or return object. This led to an unreliable division of work in the old proposal: conservatively add less waiting on the Secret side, and conservatively add fewer fields on the directory side. This “change a little less on both sides” trade-off did not provide comparable failure scenarios.

The related entry points examined later were APH-207 and APH-224, respectively. The former only required recording what “Secret version timing” actually returned or threw through the public entry point; the latter required checking matching and non-matching cases using the repository's own paths. They separated the two issues, but this page did not use that separation to form a new unified conclusion. In particular, a single match cannot show that all nested directories will be preserved correctly, and a single Secret return cannot show that use immediately afterward will necessarily be stable.

## Candidate Approaches During Review

There were three options for version timing at the time.

1. Keep the old draft: proceed directly to the subsequent Secret flow after the creation call returns. The advantage is that the calling interface remains unchanged; the disadvantage is the weakest failure attribution.
2. Wait only when the return indicates an asynchronous operation. The advantage is that waiting is limited to paths that need it; the disadvantage is that it first requires clarifying which information in the returned object represents an operation that can be waited on, and what still needs to be checked after waiting ends.
3. Split creation and subsequent access into two user-visible steps. The advantage is clear error locations; the disadvantage is a longer command interaction, with callers also having to handle state across two stages.

The old draft chose the first option and left the second for “adding later if problems arise”. This ordering was unreasonable: the second option depends not on a new requirement that only appears after an exception occurs, but on completion semantics that should have been confirmed from the outset. The third option never entered implementation discussions only because there was no desire at the time to expand the command changes, not because it had been proven unusable.

There were also three ways to handle the root directory: rely entirely on the repository's default directory; pass through a nested directory unchanged whenever the caller supplies one; or validate that directory before constructing the creation request. The old draft favored the second, but did not clearly distinguish between an empty directory, a relative directory, and the repository root directory. The first is sufficient for simple repositories, but loses the application location already known to the caller; the third makes it easier to report errors early, but adds path checks and compatibility branches.

One counterexample that was not addressed at the time is retained here: an application subdirectory exists in the repository, but the caller does not explicitly supply a directory value. The old proposal would classify this as a default layout; whether the actual creation target would still be correct was not recorded at the time. Another class of counterexamples is a caller-supplied value that points to a non-application directory within the repository. The old proposal did not specify whether to reject it, fall back to the root directory, or continue creating.

## An Unfinished Recheck

When APH-224 later moved into review, the recorded reason was that implementation had been completed on an existing branch, so it was moving directly to review. This shows that the directory path was no longer merely a longer-term option in the proposal; however, it did not establish whether Secret timing had been addressed at the same time, nor did it provide evidence that both were covered by the same change. The old page had previously misrepresented “the implementation is near the creation path” as “they can be accepted together”; that judgment should be marked as outdated.

The recheck did not produce a new assertion to replace the old proposal. The existing records support only two things: the actual behavior of version operations needs to be recorded separately, and matches and non-matches in repository path checks need to be recorded separately. They cannot be merged into one set of pass criteria, much less can the directory-side review status be used to vouch for the Secret side.

## Provisional Closeout Position

If this proposal is still used for verification, first split Secret and directories into two records. The Secret record should stay within the scope of the points where the creation call returns, subsequent actions begin, and failures appear; the directory record should retain both a request using the default directory and a request supplying a nested directory. When both are insufficient, the old judgments of “return means completion” or “pass it through whenever there is a value” should no longer be used.

The originally planned rollback approach should also be split. If version access is found to occur before creation has stabilized, roll back only the arrangement that proceeds directly to subsequent actions; if the creation target is found not to preserve the application directory, roll back only the assumption that the directory can be defaulted. Do not change the behavior of one because of an anomaly in the other.

This page has not been updated into a new interface decision. It preserves a combined proposal that was convenient during one round of closeout, but whose boundaries were not clear enough. If the background needs to be reconstructed later, start separately with the actual return records in APH-207 and the path-check records in APH-224.

# Recovery troubleshooting tree: no Backend

When recovering a deployment, first confirm whether you're seeing “no Backend selected” or whether the project actually has no available Backend. The old notes handled these two cases and a missing Compute account in the same path. That combined assessment remains below; once you find an actual Backend, don't use it to infer the account's status.

From the deployment entry point, refer back to `src/deploy/functions/backend.ts`. First record the project and location selected for this attempt, along with the Backend name entered. These values are more useful than the generic terminal messages when you re-enter the creation or selection flow.

- If the query returns a Backend, stop following the “no Backend” recovery path. Return to service account resolution for that Backend and confirm whether the runtime account has been obtained. Don't substitute the Cloud Build default identity just because the default Compute account is missing. The two types of identity were separate in the implementation at the time.
- If no Backend is returned, first return to the Backend creation flow, retaining the project, location, and repository selections. Don't grant Secret access or start a rollout before the Backend has been created; the resulting access grant would not establish which backend it was intended for.
- If the creation or query flow has established the Backend but the Compute account is still missing, retrieve the project number again and check whether the default Compute identity has appeared. The old approach treated this step as the criterion for completed creation. It can only indicate that recovery is not yet complete; it cannot prove that Backend creation failed.
- If the account still hasn't appeared, stop at the identity check and record the project number, location, Backend name, and raw failure output from this attempt. Don't borrow the Cloud Build identity as a temporary substitute or create another Backend with the same name.

The old sequence of “restore the Compute account first, then continue with all subsequent actions” is no longer accurate enough: if a Backend exists, first confirm the runtime account it actually uses; if no Backend exists, there is no target for the access grant. This page is retained because it can still help keep the two branches distinct, but it does not cover deleted backends, backends with the same name in different regions, or explicitly configured service accounts. If you encounter any of these cases, stop at the Backend query results and do not apply this page's recovery logic.

For this round's GA closeout, record the managed Secret's ownership tag separately from the release action. The previous practice was to proceed with the release as soon as the Secret appeared usable; ownership information, the IAM update, and rollout were completed in the same operation, making it difficult to tell which stage had become stuck when something went wrong.

The post-migration sequence is provisionally three steps: first confirm that the item being handled is a managed Secret and record its ownership tag; then initiate the required access authorization; only then start rollout. Here, “last” refers to the operation order; it does not mean that permissions are immediately available after the IAM request returns. The initial version does not contain enough records to determine how the waiting window should be assessed.

Do not delete the old path yet. If the new sequence cannot confirm before rollout whether authorization has taken effect, retain the original release entry point and mark that operation as pending review. Do not conflate a missing tag and permission propagation as the same failure.

# Managed Secret Release Migration Process

The first version linked Secret ownership labels, authorization updates, and rollout into a single sequence of operations, making it easy to remember but unsuitable for review. During later revisions, we found that callers actually need each of the three stages recorded separately: the label answers “who owns this managed Secret”, IAM answers “whether access has been submitted”, and rollout answers “at which step the release begins”. These three answers should not be replaced by a single success or failure message.

## Operating Guidelines Before and After Migration

The old approach usually started with the release command. As long as the Secret already existed, it proceeded directly to rollout; if a later step failed, the record often contained only “the release did not continue”. This way of recording things obscures two issues: whether the ownership label had been determined before starting, and whether time was allowed between completion of the IAM write and the permissions taking effect on the relevant services.

Now migrate according to the following boundaries:

1. Before authorization, confirm that the object being handled is a managed Secret, and save the ownership label observed at that time. The label identifies the object at this step; do not use it to infer that IAM has taken effect.
2. Authorize access to the Secret. After submitting the authorization, do not immediately treat the start of rollout as the authorization result.
3. Wait for IAM to propagate, and separately record any status or failure stage available during the wait.
4. Start rollout only after this propagation check is complete. The release record should distinguish between “rollout has not yet started” and “rollout has started but has not completed”.

This does not require copying a large record for every release. A routine migration only needs to put the label, authorization submission, and rollout start point together in one record that can be consulted later; for migrations with exceptions, also retain the failure stage and downloadable artifacts. This prevents an object selection error before authorization from being mistaken for a rollout issue during a later review.

## Retaining the Old Entry Point

The old entry point can still serve as a recovery path, but it should no longer skip the label check. During recovery, first stop before rollout: confirm that the Secret's ownership label matches the target of this release, then resubmit access authorization. If the propagation status of IAM cannot yet be determined, do not start a new rollout; what is being restored here is the ability to operate through the old entry point, not the old sequence of “release first, explain later”.

The first version's rule that “the release can continue as soon as the Secret is seen to be available” no longer applies. Secret availability only means that the object itself can be found; it cannot replace confirmation of authorization propagation. This correction comes from the scope of this round of compatibility checks and should not be extended into a conclusion covering all Secret Manager scenarios.

## Review Records

APH-209 is used to fill in the visible difference in managed Secret ownership labels between successful and failed calls. The card was first included in the release scope and then processed; it is not an independent source for determining whether a rollout can start.

APH-226 records the routine integration for starting a rollout after IAM propagation. The risk review and subsequent processing have already taken place, but the card action itself provided neither a propagation window nor the result of any particular rollout. Therefore, this page retains the gap of “waiting to determine how,” rather than using the card status to fill in a specific duration or success criteria.

## Where to Look

The legacy navigation related to Secret points to `src/functions/secrets.ts`. Near this file, `utils`, `operation-poller`, and imports for Cloud Functions v1 and v2 are visible; when investigating a release stoppage, start here to look for Secret operations and adjacent polling, but do not use this as a basis for attributing all rollout orchestration to this file.

Another set of checks for build identity and runtime identity is at DOC-22. It shares the release context with this page, but does not replace this page’s record of ownership labels, IAM propagation, and rollout order.

# Managed Secret Release Migration Workflow

During the GA wrap-up, managed Secret issues are especially likely to be recorded as a single “release failure”: someone sees incorrect labels, someone sees that authorization has just been submitted, and someone is already waiting for rollout. Once these fragments are put in the same result field, the next investigation can only start over and guess how far the process had gotten. This record preserves the migration process, focusing on two adjacent but distinct concerns: ownership labels for managed Secrets, and the sequence of starting rollout only after IAM propagation is complete.

The earliest release path had no explicit stopping point. After confirming that a Secret existed, operators would add authorization and continue the release in the same operation. This approach was brief when everything went smoothly, but failures left behind a conflated outcome: there was no way to tell whether the Secret being handled was the intended managed Secret, or whether rollout had started before authorization propagated or had started and then stalled. Based on this, the first version proposed “separate labeling, authorization, and release into three steps,” but there was still no way to determine propagation status at the time.

The later work to organize routine adoption did not fill this gap with a fixed wait time. Waiting for IAM propagation is not a timer-based action; what needs to be checked is the status after authorization submission, and whether rollout has not yet started. Without both of these, “we have already waited a while” cannot justify proceeding. The current migration guidance therefore retains an explicit stopping point: after updating authorization, check propagation first; if propagation cannot be determined, stop before rollout.

## Misleading Guidance Left by the Old Path

The following passage captures the original intent of a side note in the first version. It is retained because some old operation records still follow this interpretation:

> Once the Secret can be found, the release can be started first, and authorization can be checked afterward based on the release result.

This passage is obsolete. It compresses object existence, Secret ownership, the IAM write, and permission propagation into a single “safe to proceed” signal. During the actual migration, being able to find a Secret only means that object verification can begin. It does not mean that the selected Secret's ownership labels have been confirmed, much less that the relevant access permissions have taken effect for the identity used by rollout.

Another old habit is to treat ownership labels as incidental text in release logs. This loses their most useful function: identifying the managed Secret targeted by the current operation before authorization. Labels do not determine IAM, nor do they determine rollout success; they simply allow subsequent records to distinguish object selection from permission propagation. The requirement to retain separate label snapshots for successful and failed calls is still being tracked in APH-209.

## Sequence After Migration

The migration does not require reworking all Secret operations. It only constrains this path involving managed Secrets and App Hosting releases. Follow this sequence:

**Verify the object first.** When the managed Secret to be handled is found, record the visible ownership labels. The question to answer here is “which object does this authorization and release target”. If labels are missing or cannot be matched to the release target, stop the operation here; do not start rollout first to test whether the object is correct.

**Then submit access authorization.** Record the authorization action separately as submitted. At this point, the record should not say “release is ready,” because completing the IAM write and completing permission propagation are not the same thing. If the authorization action itself fails, preserve the fact that the failure occurred during the authorization stage; do not classify it as part of rollout.

**Wait and check propagation.** This stage does not end after a universal number of seconds. Check whatever propagation status is available, or explicitly record that the status cannot yet be determined. Do not proceed to rollout without a propagation determination. This stopping point may look like an extra step compared with the old path, but it prevents authorization that has not yet propagated from being misrecorded as a release orchestration issue.

**Finally, start rollout.** Record the start of rollout as a separate event. This makes it possible to distinguish two types of failure: one where the process stopped before rollout, possibly because of object verification, authorization submission, or propagation status; and another where rollout has already started, requiring further investigation along the release and operation-polling path. “Deployment failed” must not be used to cover both cases.

This path can be condensed into the following operational sketch:

```text
Old path
Secret exists ──> Submit authorization ──> Immediate rollout
                    │
                    └── All three stages are conflated on failure

Current path
Verify ownership labels ──> Submit IAM update ──> Check propagation ──> Start rollout
     │                    │               │
     └── Stop if object is unclear     └── Stop if submission fails └── Stop if status is unclear
```

“Stop” in the diagram does not declare the release permanently failed. It prohibits using the next stage's results to explain the previous stage. For example, if labels do not match, authorization should not proceed; if authorization was not submitted successfully, rollout should not start; if propagation is unclear, rollout should not be used as a tool to detect whether propagation is complete.

## Recording Migration Batches

When migrating old callers for the first time, there is no need to reconstruct all historical release records. Simply start with entry points that still handle managed Secrets and record the new sequence in the operation records. Retain at least four stage-specific details each time:

- Whether the Secret currently being handled has the expected ownership labels;
- Whether the IAM update has been submitted, or at which stage submission failed;
- The status obtained from the propagation check, or why it cannot be determined for now;
- Whether rollout has not yet started, has started, or what failure stage occurred after it started.

These four points are not a pass checklist. Each corresponds to a point where the migration may branch. A call with unclear labels does not need to continue collecting rollout logs; a call with unknown propagation status does not need to pretend it has entered the release stage either. Conversely, records for a rollout that has started should retain the locations of its subsequent artifacts, so that the next investigation does not have to start over from Secret authorization.

The scope of APH-226 is to integrate “start Rollout after IAM propagation” into maintainers' routine release workflow, and to record failure stages separately from downloadable artifacts. This card has undergone risk review and work has started, but the existing records do not provide a fixed propagation duration, specific commands, or a complete successful example. This page therefore does not prescribe how long to wait or interpret “downloadable artifacts” as any particular type of file; the migration only requires retaining them separately from the failure stage.

APH-209 instead retains an operational inventory of managed Secret ownership labels: successful and failed calls should each leave visible results. Do not assume in advance that failed calls necessarily lack labels, and do not infer from successful calls that all managed Secrets use the same labels. Its purpose is to make object identification traceable, not to replace determinations about IAM or rollout.

## Restoring the Old Entry Point

The old entry point is still retained so that release operations can return to a usable starting point when the new sequence cannot be completed, not to restore the old decision-making approach. Recovery starts before rollout:

1. Return to Secret object verification and confirm that the managed Secret involved in this operation has not been confused with the ownership label records.
2. If the previous IAM update was not submitted or failed, handle the authorization stage again; do not directly label the original failure as a rollout failure.
3. If authorization has been submitted but propagation still cannot be confirmed, remain at the propagation check rather than bypassing this stage by starting rollout early.
4. Restart rollout only after the propagation check is complete, and record this start separately from the previous record in which rollout did not start or failed.

Recovery records should explicitly state whether “rollout never started” or “rollout started and now needs a retry”. The former has no release orchestration result to interpret; only the latter requires saving artifacts related to the release stage. Previously, combining these two cases caused recovery actions to sometimes resubmit IAM and sometimes skip object verification.

If the migration reveals that the label records do not match the actual release target, simply return to object selection; do not continue with IAM or rollout. If the labels match and authorization has been submitted, but propagation status cannot be confirmed, retain that status and wait for a later determination; do not arbitrarily rewrite it as “insufficient permissions” or “rollout service failure”. These are different diagnostic directions.

## Relationship to Code Navigation

The old investigation notes direct the issue name and call name to `src/functions/secrets.ts`. The following direct dependencies are visible near that file:

```ts
import * as utils from "../utils";
import * as poller from "../operation-poller";
import * as gcfV1 from "../gcp/cloudfunctions";
import * as gcfV2 from "../gcp/cloudfunctionsv2";
```

This navigation is suitable for starting from Secret operations to inspect adjacent tool calls and operation polling. It should not be taken as a conclusion that “all release logic is here”: this page is concerned with how the migration sequence is recorded in practice, not with assigning implementation ownership to that file. When investigating a rollout that has already started, continue from the code adjacent to `operation-poller` to find the actual polling location; if the issue is still at the label or IAM propagation stage, first return to the three prerequisite stages on this page rather than immediately broadening the search to release failure.

DOC-22 retains another adjacent verification task: distinguishing Cloud Build identities and passing through the Backend runtime identity. Both pages may be opened during the same release preparation, but their records serve different purposes: this page does not borrow the other page's identity conclusions as a substitute for Secret ownership labels, nor does it use this page's propagation stopping point to infer build or runtime identities. When both need investigation, first use this page to determine whether rollout is allowed to start, then go to DOC-22 to review the separate identity-side records.

## Operational Evidence Still to Be Added

The current guidance has clarified the sequence; what is still missing is reusable operational examples. The next time a successful call occurs, add the actual records linking ownership labels, the IAM submission point, the propagation check, and the rollout start point; the next time a call fails, first identify which stage it stopped at. In particular, cases where “authorization has been submitted but propagation cannot be determined” must not be reduced afterward to a vague release-failure label.

The changes in this record stop here: labels identify the object, IAM propagation is a prerequisite check for rollout, and rollout itself is recorded separately from the moment it starts. The old path can restore the operational entry point, but it no longer restores the sequence of starting a release first and interpreting permission status afterward.

versions.body:
# App Hosting Identity Evolution Record

This record originally addressed a naming confusion. Around Backend creation, it was common to mention both the Developer Connect proxy domain and the default identities for Compute and Cloud Build. It was not unusual for them to be written side by side in meetings: all were related to App Hosting work in the same project, and all could appear during troubleshooting as account or service names. The problem was that appearing side by side made them easy to interpret as having the same source, and then as identities available at the same stage.

The initial draft took a straightforward approach: instead of defining a “project default account” that covered every situation, it first retained the service that each name belonged to in the record. This decision did not resolve every kind of permissions, creation, or runtime anomaly; it only prevented troubleshooters from using one name to stand in for another. In hindsight, this scope is narrower than the wording in the initial draft suggested, but it remains the part of this old record worth preserving.

## Trade-offs in the Initial Draft

There were three possible ways to write it at the time.

| Approach | Benefit at the time | Reason it was not adopted or was retained |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Record the proxy domain, Compute, and Cloud Build uniformly as the project default identity | The note in the creation path would be brief | Names at the same level do not imply the same service source, and anomalies would lose their point of reference. |
| Choose one preferred account only at Backend creation | It appeared to concentrate the decision at the entry point | The creation entry alone cannot explain what the subsequent build and runtime stages each depend on. |
| Record clues separately by service name, then trace them back through adjacent implementations | The notes would be more fragmented | Adopted. More fragmented, but it would not turn the proxy domain into an alias for a build or runtime account. |

The first approach was the easiest to misuse later. It treated “default” as a property that could propagate across services: after finding an account that looked reasonable, people assumed it could also explain the other stages. The initial draft did not prove that this propagation was valid, so it did not make it part of the decision. The second approach was also set aside. Backend creation is an entry point that needs attention, but its existence cannot replace an assessment of the boundaries between build and runtime.

The third approach that was retained is not a complete identity model. It is more like a work sequence: first confirm whether the discussion concerns the Developer Connect proxy domain, the Compute default identity, or the Cloud Build default identity; then decide which side’s implementation or runtime records to inspect. The cost is that the same issue leaves several short notes instead of one seemingly complete unified conclusion. The initial draft chose to bear that cost.

## Previous Judgment and Its Problems

The initial draft described “the proxy domain has already appeared” too much like an exclusion condition, as if the presence of a name on the Developer Connect side meant that the default identity issue could be set aside temporarily. That sentence was not deleted because it explains why some people checked Developer Connect first at the time; however, it is no longer suitable for judging service readiness.

The proxy domain is a connection clue for Developer Connect. The Compute and Cloud Build default identities, by contrast, are names raised in different service contexts. They can be asked about together in the same Backend creation task, but they cannot replace one another merely because they belong to the same project. The shared label in the initial draft made discussion easier, but the cost was that it brought “seeing a name” too close to “confirming that the identity is used at a particular stage.”

Another old practice should also be preserved as it was: when an identity anomaly occurs, first look for an explicit value near the configuration, then use that value to explain creation, build, and runtime behavior. This can occasionally narrow down the issue, but it enlarged the local meaning of an explicit service account. The existing record does not support the claim that “an explicit value overrides all stages.” The earlier paragraph that treated it as a unified priority is preserved as a previous judgment and is no longer a basis for a new review.

## Clues Left by the File Review

The subsequent review returned to `src/gcp/devConnect.ts`. The file header directly imports `Client`, and also imports `developerConnectOrigin` and `developerConnectP4SAOrigin`. These three names appear in the same local adjacency, which is why this record continues to retain that file as an entry point for Developer Connect verification.

What is most useful here is not the filename itself, but that the two origin names were not folded into generalized default-identity naming. `developerConnectOrigin` and `developerConnectP4SAOrigin` allow the Developer Connect side to continue to be identified separately. The review therefore pulled back the broader wording in the initial draft: the proxy domain is not another way of writing an arbitrary default account, nor should it be replaced by a project-level account conclusion.

This review did not interpret the import of `Client` as the complete responsibility for Backend creation, nor did it infer a call order from the two origin names. All the file header can establish is that the current file is adjacent to the API client, the Developer Connect service entry point, and its P4SA entry point. For an evolution record, this is enough to correct the name classification; it is not enough to write all creation, build, and runtime relationships as established implementation behavior.

To prevent the old notes from merging the three types of clues again, the status sketch from that time was retained. It describes the branches at registration time, not a service call graph.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Name source pending verification" as Pending
    state "Developer Connect proxy domain" as DevConnect
    state "Compute default identity" as Compute
    state "Cloud Build default identity" as CloudBuild

    [*] --> Pending
    Pending --> DevConnect : proxy domain
    Pending --> Compute : default identity
    Pending --> CloudBuild : default identity
```

The three endpoints in the diagram do not indicate execution order, nor do they indicate that any two of them can be interchanged. The diagram simply depicts the recording action decided on in the initial draft: when the same phrase, “default identity,” appears, it cannot stop at the shared label; it must first be assigned to the side that owns the corresponding name.

## Revised Decision

The decision retained on this page is now stated in four points.

First, record the Developer Connect proxy domain separately as a Developer Connect clue. It can direct verification to `src/gcp/devConnect.ts`, but it cannot replace confirmation of the Compute or Cloud Build default identity.

Second, record the Compute and Cloud Build default identities separately. Both contain the word “default,” but that does not provide a basis for converting one into the other. The presence, absence, or explicit configuration on one side cannot directly establish the state of the other side.

Third, the Backend creation record is responsible only for describing the names and selections observed at creation; it must not infer anything for the build or runtime stages. When discussion of a particular stage needs to continue, the stage name and service name should be written together, rather than adding a vague statement that “the default account has been confirmed.”

Fourth, file review should prioritize locally visible object names. For Developer Connect issues, `developerConnectOrigin` and `developerConnectP4SAOrigin` are more suitable starting points for tracing back than generalized account terms. If a new implementation location later takes over these names, add the explanation at that location instead of expanding this page into a summary of all identity paths.

These four points revise the wording of the initial draft but do not overturn its core trade-off: names from different services cannot be combined into a project-level fact merely because they belong to the same App Hosting project. The quicker judgments in the old text can still help readers understand why the source of the name was checked first at the time; they simply can no longer be treated as directly executable identity-determination rules.

## Outdated Parts Still Retained

This record still uses “separate Compute and Cloud Build default identities” as its discussion topic. The topic is useful for reminding readers not to merge the two clues, but it does not provide complete identity rules for each service in every situation. Earlier materials described it as a process that could cover creation, build, and runtime, which was an overextension and is no longer applicable.

The troubleshooting order of “find the easiest account to see first” is similarly outdated. When configuration is missing, it may produce a candidate value, but a candidate value is not a conclusion. If the name comes from Developer Connect, it only indicates that the Developer Connect side is worth examining further; if the name is called the Compute or Cloud Build default identity, it can only first be returned to its respective service context and should not be casually assigned to the other line.

This page has not been reorganized into a current configuration guide. It preserves the evolution of a decision during the closeout of GA: first, a shared label was used to make discussion easier; then it became clear that the shared label concealed the source, so the recording method was changed to separate tracks. For people who still reference the old notes, this is more useful than leaving only the final conclusion, because it shows which statements came from early convenience and which were narrowed after the file review.

## Boundary with Adjacent Topics

The default repository path for Backend creation and the Secret authorization-region selection are adjacent topics, but they are not decided by this page. They may likewise involve service names or accounts, but each has its own creation parameters and authorization choices. Mixing these topics into the identity evolution would recreate the substitution relationship that the initial draft tried to avoid.

This page retains only one reusable way of making the determination: when a neighboring topic includes the names Developer Connect, Compute, or Cloud Build, first identify which service line the name belongs to; only if the topic itself requires it should you continue asking about its relationship to Backend creation, build, or runtime. This prevents a local entry point from being expanded into an identity conclusion for the entire project.

What remains unresolved is the scope of an explicit service account’s coverage across different stages. The existing file review did not answer this question, so “explicit account takes priority” was not included in the decision. If material about a specific stage is added later, first state what it covers, then determine whether the boundary retained here needs to be changed.

# Same-name Backend Region Troubleshooting Tree

When multiple Backends with the same name appear during a release, do not select an object by name alone. The name only narrows the candidates; the region is the second condition for this investigation. Record the Backend name provided by the caller, the target region, and the final returned status together before moving on to code review.

## Split into two cases first

**Region provided**

1. Reproduce candidate filtering with the name and region together.
2. If only one candidate remains, continue verifying that the object received by the caller is that candidate; do not skip the return-value check just because the names match.
3. If more than one candidate remains, stop automatic selection. Record the region of each candidate and return to the caller side for input that can distinguish the objects.

**No region provided**

1. First confirm that same-name candidates actually exist in the environment, rather than that old output was mixed into the list result.
2. When multiple candidates exist, do not treat the first result in the list as the answer. Have the caller specify the target region, then retry.
3. Even with only one candidate, retain the scope of this list result; if another region is added later, the same name may no longer be unique.

## Code review

The current navigation entry is `src/deploy/functions/backend.ts`. When reviewing it, follow the Backend filtering logic downward, focusing on how `region` participates in filtering and which branches contain `matches`, `list`, `message`, and the returned `object`, respectively. The goal here is to identify the branches for “no match,” “unique match,” and “duplicate name,” not to infer ownership of a deployment command's implementation from the filename.

The top of the file also imports `../../gcp/cloudfunctions`, `../../gcp/cloudfunctionsv2`, `../../utils`, and `./runtimes/supported`. When candidates come from different generations of functions, record their sources separately first; do not merge same-name results from two entry points into one Backend.

## Stop conditions

If any of the following cannot be confirmed, do not continue making the region selection for the release:

- The caller has not provided the target region;
- There are more than two same-name candidates in the list;
- The returned object cannot be matched to a recorded candidate;
- The branch being reviewed does not show whether `message` handles no match or multiple matches.

The investigation record must include at least the name, region, candidate count, and actual returned status. This makes it possible to determine, the next time a same-name object appears, whether the input is missing a region or the filtering branch itself does not include the region in the match.

# Build and Runtime Account Grouping Proposal

GA During the closeout phase, start with a simple assumption: builds and runtime for the same Backend use the same group of accounts, with only one selection in the configuration flow. This avoids having to explain the differences between the build and runtime sides separately during creation, and Secret authorization can reuse the same selection.

There are two candidate approaches.

- Merged grouping: Select one group of accounts when creating the Backend, and take the values for both build and runtime from that selection.
- Separate grouping: Record the build account and runtime account separately during creation, then expand the authorization steps by purpose.

The initial draft leans toward merged grouping. This is not because the two types of tasks are considered identical, but because the most likely problem during closeout is that users know only the Backend name and not which side needs additional configuration. Splitting the selection into two parts would make the interaction, configuration, and troubleshooting entry points longer; merging them first keeps the issue scoped to the Backend level.

The trade-off is clear: once the build and runtime accounts actually have different permissions, the merged name will hide that distinction. The current draft still assumes this difference will occur only in a small number of special projects, with exceptions added when they arise rather than changing the default flow to use two groups.

The recommendation is to use the same grouping result at the creation and Secret setup entry points first. If a Backend later turns out to require separate account specifications, revert this merge: retain the Backend identifier, add separate build-side and runtime-side fields, and populate both existing configurations with the original selection. It has not yet been decided whether the exception should be exposed during creation or whether users should be asked to fill it in only after authorization fails.

# Build and Runtime Account Grouping Proposal

The initial draft treated “only one account group is needed for the same Backend” as the default consolidation approach. That judgment remains here: at the time, it addressed the problem of too many entry points, rather than establishing the responsibilities of the accounts. During a later review, the file originally treated as the wiring point provided narrower clues than expected; the draft was not rewritten into a two-account proposal on that basis, so both the old choice and its blind spots have been retained.

## Choices Left by the Initial Draft

The original plan was to put build and runtime accounts in the same group. When creating a Backend, the operator would make only one account selection; Secret settings would reuse the same result. The benefits were a shorter workflow and the ability to use the Backend name as the sole lookup target. The initial draft was especially concerned about another situation: users already knew which Backend they wanted to change, but were required to first distinguish whether the configuration issue was “on the build side or the runtime side.” Merging the groups deferred that distinction so configuration could proceed to completion first.

The other option listed at the time was to separate them from the first step. The build account would be recorded separately, the runtime account would be recorded separately, and any step that depended on an account would read it according to its purpose. The advantage was straightforward field meanings; the disadvantage was having to explain where the two selections came from during initial configuration, and having to decide which side an existing set of values should go to when migrating old configurations. The initial draft did not design migration rules, and simply assumed that most Backends did not need this distinction.

That assumption is the draft's central risk. It treated “there should be fewer configuration entry points” as sufficient justification for “accounts can be shared.” Without counterexamples, this inference looks convenient; with counterexamples, the proposal itself has no place to represent them, leaving callers to add ad hoc checks.

## Scope Observed During Review

This review started by looking back at `src/deploy/functions/backend.ts`. The file header directly imports `../../gcp/cloudfunctions`, `../../gcp/cloudfunctionsv2`, `../../utils`, and `Runtime` exported by `./runtimes/supported`. These adjacent dependencies show that the file touches both function deployment and runtime types; it does not provide a field table that can be used directly to group App Hosting build and runtime accounts.

The initial draft treated this path as the center of the grouping wiring because both issue names and call names had pointed here. After review, the only thing that can be confirmed is that it is a suitable place to continue looking for adjacent deployment-side code; these imports do not establish that account selection has already been completed here. In particular, the presence of `Runtime` shows, at most, that runtime types are locally visible; it does not indicate that runtime and build accounts should be shared, nor that the two have already been separated.

The toolchain-pinning action in APH-217 allows this review to continue on the same toolchain, but the card itself does not supply the source of the account fields. Thus, two premises of the old proposal remain unverified: whether the Backend already stores both types of accounts, and whether the result obtained from Secret settings can distinguish build use from runtime use.

## Wiring Still Proposed Under the Old Approach

The draft provisionally uses the Backend as the grouping key, rather than placing accounts directly in project-level defaults. Each creation or modification first locates the target Backend, then retrieves that Backend's account-group result. This at least prevents different Backends from overwriting one another through project-level defaults, and matches the initial draft's interaction assumption that “the user knows the Backend name first.”

In this model, the build workflow reads the grouping result and then starts the build; runtime configuration uses the same result. Secret-related entry points also grant authorization only to this set of results. The grouping object's name can remain neutral, without being labeled “build account” or “runtime account” in the configuration interface, because the initial draft's premise is precisely that the two sides are not separated for now.

The proposed workflow does not require turning `backend.ts` into the sole entry point. That file is the starting point for this review, and both function deployment and runtime dependencies can be traced further from here; where account selection takes place still needs to be confirmed along the call relationships. To keep the workflow name from obscuring this gap, the draft recommends retaining only two checks before wiring: whether the target has been resolved to a specific Backend, and whether the retrieved account result is empty. It does not define which type of default identity should be selected automatically when the result is empty.

If later implementation finds that the same Backend already has two distinguishable account sources, the old proposal would still favor collapsing them into one group. This is not because having two sources is meaningless, but because the initial draft gave compatibility with old configurations more weight than accurately expressing purpose. After collapsing them, callers would not need to add two sets of parameters immediately either; the cost is that, during troubleshooting, the group name cannot indicate whether a failure belongs to build or runtime.

## Trade-offs Accepted at the Time

Merging the groups would broaden the scope of authorization. The initial draft accepted this, considering configuration omissions, rather than confusion over permissions, to be the main source of failures during consolidation. It therefore put “being able to complete a Backend configuration” ahead of “explaining each account by purpose.” This ordering was not validated against actual permission differences, and no exception list was developed for different Backends.

Separating the groups would instead trade the risk for migration costs. If an existing Backend has only one account value, splitting it requires choosing whether to copy it into both fields, write it only to the build side, or write it only to the runtime side. All three migrations could change existing behavior; the initial draft did not want to introduce this choice while consolidating GA, so it did not adopt the separation approach.

There was also a third compromise: keep one account group on the surface, store separate build and runtime slots internally, and fall back to the shared value only when a slot is missing. This would leave an interface for future separation, but would leave invisible precedence rules even after configuration was complete. The initial draft considered this implicit fallback harder to troubleshoot than an explicit single-group rule, so it did not list it as the default approach.

## Conditions for Withdrawal

If investigation finds that build and runtime retrieve accounts from different sources, and one side cannot safely reuse the other side's account, the merged grouping should be withdrawn. When withdrawing it, the Backend should not be removed as the lookup key; only the results within the group should be split into build and runtime values, with new configurations required to fill them in explicitly. Old configurations should retain the shared value initially, with the decision about which side to write it to, or whether to copy it to both sides, deferred until migration.

If the problem is only that a particular call entry point does not pass the Backend down, that does not establish a need for two groups. For that type of problem, restoring Backend lookup is enough as a first step. Conversely, if the account result is empty, that empty value cannot be interpreted directly as a reason to merge; it may come from the selection chain, missing configuration, or failure to locate the correct Backend yet.

The most troublesome issue after withdrawal would be Secret authorization. The initial draft assumed that it could reuse the shared result; after separation, it must be made explicit whether authorization is for the build account, the runtime account, or both. There is no usable migration conclusion here, so the shared value cannot be expanded automatically into two authorizations without first confirming their purposes.

## Questions Still Unresolved

- After `src/deploy/functions/backend.ts`, the actual call site through which account selection enters has still not been recorded in this draft.
- There is no conclusion yet on whether `Runtime` and account selection are on the same configuration chain.
- After the toolchain is pinned in APH-217, the specific configuration file in which missing build configuration items should be placed still needs to be checked separately.
- If separation is required, the draft has not decided whether the shared account value of an old Backend should be copied, migrated, or require a new selection.

What is retained here is therefore an old proposal that prioritizes reducing entry points, not a final account of account responsibilities.

# Caller Entry-Point Traceback Flow

This page preserves an old handoff path. “current” in the entry filename refers to the revision being viewed when it was written; it should not be understood as the project’s only current entry point: `docs/adj-commands/notes/from-current-entry-go-to-current-revision.md` can still help people find the source material, but it was not reorganized as subsequent integrations changed.

The original notes had only two reference points: `IAM propagation`, followed immediately by `apphosting.yaml`. At the time, the intent was to trace directly to `Firebase CLI` because that name also appeared nearby; only later, on review, did it become clear that the call edge in between was missing. The old draft placed the three in a row, making it easy to assume that they already formed the sequence of entry, configuration, and execution. In reality, all that remains is their proximity within the same replay.

## Starting from the Original Sample

The constraints around APHA-005 are narrow: replay the original commands-client-integration, rather than reconstructing a similar input. The distinction here is that the caller integration record preserves the objects and order of appearance from the actual sample. Rerunning it with another extension, another integration, or even a parameter with the same name produces a new state and cannot replace the first visible result on the old page.

After opening the entry page, first find the caller object associated with the replay, then check whether `IAM propagation` appears before or after the input. The notes do not provide a complete internal chain that can be expanded, so this section is only for identifying whether this is a marker left by the propagation side or by the configuration side. If the page presents it only as a side note, copy down the object adjacent to that side note; do not extend it into a complete authorization flow.

Next, look at `apphosting.yaml`. Here, it is not a declaration that “all callers must pass through” it; it is simply the project configuration filename visible in the old sample. Its value is that it helps return to the original state: when the configuration file appears again during a replay, you can compare whether it still falls within the same caller record. It does not resolve who called whom, nor can it by itself show which layer the error exited from.

The old draft’s TODO included the note “check whether the error goes out unchanged or changes type in the previous layer.” This question has never been turned into a conclusion. When an error is encountered, first preserve the original wording on the original entry page, then find the first place where its form changes; if the page does not preserve the outputs from both sides, write only “undetermined.” Inserting a backend or rollout name seen later here does not make the type change verifiable.

## Names That Should Not Be Merged

`Firebase CLI` is the name in these notes most likely to be misread. It appeared, but was not connected back to a direct caller. The old version’s statement that it “appeared once nearby” is still valid; what no longer applies is interpreting it as belonging to the entry layer. When tracing back along this old page now, seeing it should take you back to the previous entry with an actual object relationship, rather than continuing across based on the name alone.

`Cloud Build Repositories` and `Developer Connect` present the same kind of issue. They were recorded as names alongside the material, and the old page provides no connection sufficient to determine how either affected caller integration. These two names are retained so that people can return to the entry page and check the context at the time, not so that they can be turned into a migration path. If a replay encounters only one of them, record that name and the adjacent object; do not fill in missing steps for the other side.

Similarly, `location` can serve as a reading checkpoint for a location selection. It only indicates that the reader has reached the location-related section; it cannot automatically establish that the backend afterward was selected. A previous note treated “seeing location” as a signal to continue tracing the backend, but that shortcut no longer applies: without an object linked in the original sample, stop at the location selection.

## Recovery Record Beside the Old Page

APHA-007 requires the recovery result to be shown alongside the original state. The two types of material shown side by side are the inputs and objects seen in the original failure window, and the recovery result added afterward. Do not replace the failure window on the entry page with the recovered result; otherwise, later readers will see only one successful replay and will not be able to determine whether it still followed the same path.

This is also why this page does not present “recovery” as a new starting point. The recovery result should be attached beside the original entry, and the first question should be whether it still corresponds to the same commands-client-integration sample; if the object has changed, record it as a new state. The old page’s wording is fairly rough and can provide only the first fork and the traceback address; it cannot account for every integration difference.

A record related to an expiration action was once brought into this area, but it was later marked as having been put on the wrong card, and is not the same state as “the recovery result alongside the original state.” It should not be used to explain the reason for stalling, nor to add a temporal order to `IAM propagation` or `apphosting.yaml`. Keeping this correction prevents anyone from later reconstructing a nonexistent call chain backward from a card title.

## How Far Is Enough to Read

The first reliable stopping point on this old path is still `IAM propagation` and `apphosting.yaml` in the original sample. If the adjacent object between them is still present, you can continue checking whether the configuration side belongs to the same replay; if only isolated names remain, do not pretend that they are connected.

The second stopping point is `location`. When it appears, check whether the page still preserves the context of the same location selection; without context, record only the name. The third stopping point is `Firebase CLI`: the direct caller is still missing here, and the old notes have no answer.

backend, rollout, `Secret Manager`, and service identity were mentioned in a broader range of material, but they are not confirmed next hops on this page. They can be used as search terms, but not written as subsequent steps for this entry. This distinction may seem conservative, but it preserves the most useful part of the old page: it takes people from the actual caller sample back to the first fork, rather than from a string of familiar terms to an imagined chain.

Two items still remain unresolved:

- Which direct caller did `Firebase CLI` use to enter this replay;
- Whether the original error changed type in the previous layer.

If either item is later filled in on the entry page, append the new observation beside the original object; do not reorder the old paragraphs. “Current revision” in the old paragraphs is now historical wording, but the original failure window and original sample are still worth preserving.
