# Caller-Side Integration Testing: Two-State Postmortem Review

This record preserves the incident in which the same object presented two states before and after caller-side integration testing; it is not a summary that assigns all integration issues to a single cause. The object came from real call samples formed by integration and extension; it also carries the adaptation boundary and integration feedback. Initially, the page showed that the old record did not match the current entry point. The page later recovered partially, but the recovery did not erase the earlier record.

The easiest part of the incident to misread is treating "looks normal now" as "there was no difference earlier." On the first check of the entry point, the current revision in the record differed from the current revision seen on a subsequent check. Both referred to the same object, but the value ultimately displayed on the page could only describe the state at the time of viewing; it could not replace the original record. The original input, entry-point version, and recovery page were therefore retained; further retries stopped after confirming that location had recovered.

This is not a fault description for all commands. The impact is limited to the judgment based on this set of call samples: the integrator received states for the same object that could not be directly reconciled, and the original adaptation conclusion could not be established solely by the later page check. The object has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit action. This review does not list changes to other projects, the state of other services, or paths that were not reproduced as causes.

## The Short Note Left at the Time

The original short note contained only a few points: the Secret Manager observation differed from the old record; location later recovered; it was still unknown why backend had changed. That short note did not contain complete timestamps, nor did it conflate the recovery action with root-cause confirmation. Its value was not in providing an explanation, but in preserving the fact that "different states had definitely been observed before recovery."

At the time, we did not fill in details that did not exist. In particular, we did not describe a single page difference as proof that the backend had rewritten the object, nor did we extend location's recovery to mean that all integration-testing paths had recovered. The subsequent review continued under the same constraint: first distinguish the state already seen, the state seen again after recovery, and the part that still could not explain the difference between them.

The statement "Secret Manager is different from the old record" in the original record is incident language, not the final attribution. It describes an inconsistency found during comparison; it does not prove that Secret Manager itself caused the two states. The laterorganizemanage retained this sentence to show where the initial investigation began, not to promote it to a conclusion.

## Event Sequence

No reliable precise timestamps can be entered into this review, so the events are listed in chronological order without disguising the sequence as elapsed duration.

| Order | Incident state | Action taken at the time | What still cannot be determined from this |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial comparison | The current entry point did not match the old record | Saved the original input and entry-point version | Which component caused the difference |
| Object checked again | The same object gave different current revisions at two viewing points | Kept both records instead of letting the later one overwrite the earlier one | Whether there was an intermediate change between the two states that was never recorded |
| Scope narrowed | backend provided no answer that could explain the difference | Listed it separately as an unknown | Whether backend was the source of the change |
| Recovery observed | location could recover | Recorded the recovery time separately from the anomaly discovery | Whether recovery explained the earlier revision difference |
| Retries stopped | The caller path returned to a state where integration could continue | Stopped attempts that would only repeat page observations | Whether the root cause had been confirmed |
| Follow-uporganizemanage | The original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause still existed separately | Retained the three material locations | Rewriting the entire event based on a single page value |

This sequence table deliberately does not invent "which minute," "which request," or any response value that was not retained. The existing materials support only the before-and-after relationship: the inconsistency was seen first, and location recovered later; the reason for backend's change remains unknown. Separating these relationships prevents the later appearance of the recovery page from being used to retroactively deny the initial incident.

## What Each of the Two States Means

The first state came from comparing the old record with the current entry point. It was an actual observation in an integration-testing sample, not a design assumption. It temporarily removed the single basis for the original integration judgment: the caller could not know whether to rely on the current revision in the old record or the current revision subsequently displayed by the entry point.

The second state came from checking again after recovery. The recovery of location was a valid change, showing that at least the observed path had become usable again. But it answered only "whether location recovered"; it did not answer "why backend changed," nor did it show which of the two revisions represented the object's state across all adjacent paths.

Therefore, the simultaneous presence of "recovered" and "cause unknown" in the event is not contradictory. The former is an observation about a specific path; the latter is an attribution judgment about the difference between the two states. Placing the two statements too close together previously made it easy for readers to assume that recovery itself was the cause. They are separated in theorganizemanage: the recovery page records visible recovery; the unknown item records the explanatory gap.

Another easily confused point is the object versus the page. The page is the display provided by the current entry point at a particular viewing point; the old record is the incident state saved earlier. Both relate to the object, but they are not materials that can be casually substituted for each other. The page's final value can serve as corroborating evidence, but it cannot delete the original incident state. Keeping both is not intended to create a contradiction; it allows subsequent review to continue seeing that the difference once existed.

## State Flow

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> OldRecord: Retain old record
    OldRecord --> DivergenceSeen: Current entry point differs
    DivergenceSeen --> LocationRecovered: location recovered
    DivergenceSeen --> BackendUnknown: backend cause unknown
    LocationRecovered --> EvidenceKept: Retain recovery page
    BackendUnknown --> EvidenceKept: Retain unconfirmed item
    EvidenceKept --> [*]
```

The two branches in the diagram are not two independent incidents. They came from the same object during the same round of integration testing; they simply carry the already observed recovery and the change that has not yet been explained, respectively. Placing backend on the "cause unknown" side avoids a common but invalid leap: seeing it appear in the record and concluding that it caused the revision difference.

Likewise, placing location on the "recovered" side does not mean that it definitely failed at some specific layer beforehand. The existing materials show only that it could recover. Call details that were not saved should not be filled in as a failure involving an interface, configuration, permissions, or an internal service process.

## Why the Original Incident State Was Not Cleared

A page after recovery is usually easier to reopen and more likely to become the only cited material. If only that page were retained, later readers would see a usable path but not why the caller had previously stopped continuing integration based on the old record. The original incident state is retained here because the two-state condition itself is the core of this anomaly, not to preserve a page screenshot that has already been replaced.

The original input preserves the context in which the difference occurred; the entry-point version preserves the state read at the time; the recovery page preserves the fact that location later became usable. They answer different questions: the first shows where the problem was discovered, the entry-point version shows what was displayed then, and the recovery page shows which path recovered. They do not replace one another.

An earlier record tried to compress these materials into the sentence "It has recovered now." That wording was fast enough for a temporary handoff, but it could not support the next comparison: readers would not know whether different revisions had really existed before recovery, nor why backend's change remained an unknown. Version 2 no longer uses this compressed judgment.

Retaining the original record also prevents the later stable state from being written back into the initial adaptation feedback. The cautious judgment made by the caller during the anomaly concerned the entry point seen at that time; it should not be described as a false alarm because location later recovered. They are simply records from different state points.

## Scope and Impact

The affected items are the real call samples around integration and extension, together with their integration feedback. The samples are used to understand the adaptation boundary, so the state inconsistency directly affected whether the integrator could continue judging the object's state based on the current entry point. The impact does not automatically extend to all App Hosting behavior, nor does it extend to callers that did not appear in the incident.

The "impact" here does not refer to an unrecorded production consequence. What is known is that the basis for the integration judgment conflicted: the old record and the later current entry point could not be directly treated as the same result. For maintenance actions, this means that the materials from before and after recovery must be retained side by side, rather than deleting the old item first and then declaring the system normal.

The separate schedule, maintainer, and exit action are also part of the scope. This object should not be replaced by a generic status in the daily report, and changes being made by adjacent projects cannot be listed as causes of this event merely because they were happening nearby. The review retains only the state differences and integration feedback that actually occurred for this object.

The original owner must still review the exit action before it expires; if there is no new incident state, the existing exit action can be closed out based on the existing records. This action handles only the materials left by this two-state event. It does not disguise the unknown root cause as resolved, nor does it create new conclusions for adjacent objects.

## Failed Ways of Interpreting the Event

One shortcut interpretation at first was: since the recovery page already showed that location was usable, classify the event as a transient display issue. That interpretation was later withdrawn. It did not explain why the old record and the current entry point gave different current revisions, nor why backend remained an unknown. The recovery fact can be retained; attribution cannot use it to skip the question.

Another interpretation centered on backend. Because it continued to be mentioned during the comparison, it was easy to attribute the change directly to backend. This judgment also lacked sufficient material. The record preserved no fact that directly linked backend to the revision difference; writing it as the root cause would disguise an open question as a confirmed fact.

A third approach was to use only the final value on the later page. That could reduce conflict in the documentation, but it would lose the most useful part of the incident: why the caller could not continue using the old integration judgment at the earlier point in time. Version 2 explicitly does not use this cleanup approach. Leaving the original record, recovery page, and unknown cause together allows readers to reconstruct the decision boundary at the time.

These discarded interpretations are not irrelevant investigation branches. They explain why a short record is insufficient as long-term material: a short record can tell the next owner that the path recovered, but it cannot explain how the two states were discovered, which explanations were rejected, or which questions still have no answers.

## Changes in Understanding After Review

The follow-up review did not add a component that could be held responsible, but it changed how the event was organized. The materials were initially arranged around "whether the current page was normal" and were later rearranged around "anomaly discovery, recovery observation, and unknown cause." The first organization lets the later state overwrite the earlier one; the second allows the same object to retain different states at different viewing points without requiring either one to be erased first.

What the review confirmed was not a complete technical chain, but the boundary of this record: the object does belong to the independent event line of commands-client-integration; the daily report should retain only a link and should not compress the two states here into a single project status. The reason is practical: caller-side integration testing has its own real samples, adaptation boundary, integration feedback, maintainer, and exit conditions.

"Current revision" is not a static label here. It is the value given by the entry point at one viewing point. The appearance of different values at two viewing points is what constitutes the anomaly that must be documented this time. If a new value is seen again in the future, the new incident state and its relationship to the original record should be documented separately, rather than directly modifying the two observations already saved on this page.

The review also confirmed a stopping condition: as long as no new incident state can establish a connection between the difference and a specific change, we will no longer search for an answer by repeatedly checking the recovery page. Repeated checks can confirm the current display, but they cannot automatically fill in why it was different earlier. Stopping does not claim that the problem does not exist; it prevents more observations of the same kind from being fabricated into new evidence.

## Open Questions

There is still no conclusion as to why backend appears as an issue that needs to be listed separately in the before-and-after records. The existing materials do not show whether it was the source of the state change, an observation from a side path, or information that coexisted without a direct relationship to location's recovery. This question should be retained as-is rather than being covered by "the current path is usable."

The existing materials also cannot answer whether an intermediate state that was never recorded existed between the two current revisions. The review confirms only that the two viewing points differed; without intermediate material, we should not fill in a continuous change curve, much less assume that one of the readings was simply incorrect.

The recovery page can show that location recovered, but it cannot show that all adaptation boundaries have been revalidated. Extension or integration branches that did not appear in this event are not being declared passed here. If new real call samples become available later, they should be compared alongside the old incident state retained on this page, rather than using the old conclusion to replace the new observation.

Finally, the missing precise timestamps remain missing. The sequence is sufficient to support this review: the difference was discovered first, location recovered later, the cause of the backend change was unknown, and repeated retries were then stopped. There is no material supporting the duration, frequency, or intermediate actions beyond that, so leaving them blank is more faithful to the incident than turning them into a precise narrative.

## Retention Location

The maintenance entry point remains `docs/adj-commands/incidents/commands-caller-side-integration-testing-same-object-two-states.md`. This entry point retains the original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause; it does not let the page after recovery overwrite the anomaly state. If related project materials need to be linked, this review should serve as the timeline for this object rather than having the two states rewritten elsewhere.

This page may be supplemented with new actual observations during future maintenance, and confirmed causes may be appended after the unknown items; however, early observations must not be deleted to make the story neater. If the root cause is confirmed later, it should be clearly identified as a subsequent addition, while preserving the context in this version that it was "unknown at the time."

What this handling actually restored was the caller path containing location. What has not yet been restored to a definite conclusion is the explanation for the difference between the backend change and the two current revisions. # Alternative Approach to Caller Integration Testing

The discussion at the time was not about rebuilding the entire integration surface, but about separating out the callers of commands-client-integration from the existing entry point. There were two straightforward options on the table: continue keeping the caller relationships within `apphosting.yaml`, or handle `Firebase CLI` as a separate integration segment. The latter seemed more like a direction worth trying at the time, but it was not yet a decision.

Keeping the existing entry point would avoid having to split up the existing configuration first, and callers would see fewer changes. The problem was that the failure exits in the entry point's two segments did not lead to the same place: in one, processing seemed to stop on the configuration side; in the other, it looked more like the CLI side had not picked it up. Treating both as the same kind of failure and adding another branch would probably just make diagnosis take longer. That assessment came from a draft reviewed at the time, not from completed integration testing.

The idea behind splitting out CLI was to have callers first use a path that could be observed independently, while keeping the original entry point for comparison. This did not require immediately removing `apphosting.yaml`, nor should it treat the configuration file as the source of the error. The trial would check only two things: whether callers actually entered the split-out path, and whether a failure could be identified as still being in the old entry point or already in the CLI segment. If neither could be established, this approach should not become the default integration path.

Someone at the time favored shutting down the old entry point outright. I disagreed. Not because the old entry point was already reliable, but because we had not yet identified the active callers of `Developer Connect`. Cutting off the entry point first would conflate “no calls” with “callers have not caught up,” and would make it hard afterward to tell whether the split itself was the problem or whether something had been missed in the integration surface.

The tentative rollback criteria were conservative for the same reason: if the split-out path did not make the failure exits distinguishable, or if we found unlisted callers still depending on the old entry point, we would only restore the old entry point. We would not also change the meaning of the configuration or write up the trial as a rule already in effect. After restoring it, we would retain the comparison records from that time, so the next attempt would not start with guesswork at the same ambiguous entry point.

Still undecided:

- Which active callers `Developer Connect` actually had;
- Whether rollback would only restore the old entry point or also remove the CLI segment;
- Which caller to start the trial with, so that local observations would not be mistaken for shared results.

This proposal has no start date and names no one to carry it out. The earlier draft is in `docs/adj-commands/proposals/not-adopted-commands-caller-integration-testing-approach.md`; for material on the existing entry point, refer to DOC-30. This document preserves the approach that was not adopted at the time and its rollback boundaries. Later integration results should not be written back into it as conclusions already confirmed then.

# Troubleshooting tree for a stalled quality signal

When firebase-vscode-quality-signal appears stuck at the current entry point, preserve the first failing sample. Don't retry first, and don't clear existing output to trigger it again. In this signal dashboard, later output from the same test run may just be a knock-on effect of the earlier failure. Preserving the first anomaly lets us distinguish a regression-layering issue from an unstable signal.

The entry file is `docs/adj-firebase-vscode/runbooks/firebase-vscode-quality-signal-Who to hand off to when stuck.md`. First find the record containing `operation poller` here, and put the output, test log, or trace excerpts you can currently see in the same place. Record only what has actually appeared; without a trace, don't infer a runtime stage from the description.

## First branch: has it reached rollout?

**`rollout` has not been seen**

Stop at the current entry point. All we can confirm here is that the signal has not progressed to rollout. Do not attribute the issue to the backend or hand it directly to the permissions maintainer. Preserve:

- The first failing sample, not a sample from a retry;
- The complete output excerpt from this test;
- Any visible environment differences, such as whether the same signal also stalls in another environment;
- The last step shown at the current entry point.

If a new trace becomes available, reassess from this branch. Without new material, exit the investigation without taking recovery actions.

**`rollout` has been seen**

Don't clear the failure state. Check next whether `service identity` appears. The point here is not to confirm that rollout was printed, but to check whether a service identity record was left after it. In an earlier case, an immediate retry after rollout overwrote the original failing sample with the next run's output. We could no longer tell whether polling had stalled or identity information had not been returned. This kind of retry is no longer the first step.

## Second branch: has service identity appeared?

**It has not appeared**

Stop here. Record “rollout appeared; service identity did not appear” and hand it to the permissions maintenance entry point, along with the first failing sample and the environment differences. Don't fill in a service account yourself based on its absence, and don't describe this as a confirmed permissions failure. If the maintenance entry point needs new evidence, append only the output or trace it explicitly requests; preserve the existing sample unchanged.

**It has appeared**

Don't close the signal just because identity exists. Return to the original stalled behavior: if the test has continued, record that recovery occurred after identity appeared; if the test is still stuck, the issue remains with firebase-vscode-quality-signal. Include the output boundaries before and after identity in the handoff. Do not repeat the earlier recovery actions in this branch.

## How to record environment differences

Record only differences you have actually compared. For example, if one sample has rollout and another stops before the operation poller, preserve them separately rather than merging them into “the same failure.” If there are no comparable samples, write “not compared.” Don't use this environment's result as a substitute for a conclusion about another environment.

If the first failing sample has already been overwritten, save whatever output is still available, then note that the original sample is missing. Don't use a later success or failure to infer where the first run stopped. The recovery actions have not yet been tried in a shared environment. Unless there is an explicit record from the same failure state, don't treat a local rerun as confirmation of recovery.

## Exit conditions

Stop this round when any one of the following applies:

- Rollout has not appeared, and there is no new trace;
- Rollout has appeared but service identity is missing, and the failure state has been preserved and handed to the permissions maintenance entry point;
- Service identity has appeared, but the test is still stuck, and the output boundaries before and after it have been recorded;
- The first failing sample cannot be recovered, so only the available material can be saved and the gap noted.

Don't skip past the first node with missing evidence to assign a final cause. Open separate records for adjacent quality signals; don't combine them into a single conclusion in this tree.

# Release Automation Dual-State Postmortem

The issue was again the same release object showing different current revisions at two entry points. Don't reduce it to “the page briefly failed to refresh”: the build queue, artifact versions, and withdrawal window all changed around the records for `.github/workflows`. For at least part of that time, readers would infer two opposing current states from those records.

The incident was recorded in the following order. At T+00, `deploy-release automation-two states for the same object` was first observed to deviate from the baseline; the original input and entry-point version were saved. At T+07, `backend` was found to still be working normally, so the scope of impact was initially narrowed to downstream display or orchestration. At T+18, the comparison pointed to `rollout`, and the issue was routed to the corresponding maintenance path. At T+31, the user path recovered, but the root cause was not confirmed at the time of recovery.

```text
Consumer -> Release object entry point -> backend -> rollout
                       |
                       +-> Current revision in the old record
```

The initial working assessment was that, since `backend` was working normally, the queue itself was unlikely to have contributed to the discrepancy, and recovery could initially be explained as IAM propagation. The page timeline later failed to provide enough support for this assessment, but it was not removed at the time. It explains why retries were stopped, but not when the two entry points began to diverge.

Reports containing only screenshots did not help. The screenshots did not retain the account, artifact version, or run id, so they could not explain why the other path was working normally. What was added later was only the entry-point content; it cannot reconstruct the request flow that was not saved. The recovered page and the original record should be considered separately: the former shows that the user path was back, while only the latter preserves the revision seen when the divergence occurred.

When APHC-004 was reviewed later, the notes explicitly stated that the before-and-after trends in the two versions of the records could not be directly subtracted. Related follow-up notes indicated that the execution records could be reconstructed, but one section describing the current results came from an old snapshot. The old snapshot was subsequently given a version label, and the provenance chain for the execution records was displayed separately. This change did not prove that the old snapshot caused the anomaly; it only showed that treating the page text as evidence from the same point in time had been overly optimistic.

After the old-index cleanup in APHC-007, the execution records could still be opened from the historical records. In other words, deleting the old index did not mean the incident evidence was gone. This postmortem continues to leave the original records in their original location rather than rewriting them into a summary containing only the final green status.

APHC-010 required the current revision and release automation records to be reordered by their original timestamps, with the final page values used only as corroborating evidence. No missing timestamps have been filled in here, and there is no claim that the complete causal chain has been reconstructed. # Release Automation Two-State Retrospective

This record was not removed from the knowledge base because the state discrepancy between the two entry points once affected the rollback decision. Its early conclusions should no longer be treated as the troubleshooting order, but the original incident state, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause were not merged: the three describe different things from different points in time.

## The Initial Conclusion That Was Left Behind

The first record described the symptom as “Developer Connect is different from the old record.” At the time, there was no complete request context and no run id that could map the queue, artifact, and page to one another individually. Because `backend` appeared normal, the investigation was limited to the downstream side; and because the user path eventually recovered, the record stated “possibly IAM propagation.”

This wording remains here not because it is reliable, but because it did guide the on-call shift’s decision to stop: continued retries produced no new discrepancy, the original input was saved, and retries were stopped. At that time, recording recovery separately from the cause was already necessary; mistaking recovery for the cause was a problem that only became clear later.

Original entry point: `docs/adj-deploy/incidents/deploy-release-automation-same-object-has-two-states.md`. It involves the build queue, artifact version, and rollback window formed by `.github/workflows`. They belong to the same release automation object, but there is no guarantee that the “current” value on the same page came from the same read.

## Incident Timeline

| Relative time | Retained observation | Action taken |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `deploy-release-automation-same-object-has-two-states` first deviated from the baseline; the two entry points returned different current revisions | Saved the original input and entry-point versions instead of replacing them with the later page |
| T+07 | `backend` was still normal | Narrowed the impact scope first; did not directly classify the queue as the failure point |
| T+18 | Comparison data pointed to `rollout` | Handed off the follow-up check to the corresponding maintenance path |
| T+31 | The user path recovered | Ended the continuous retries; the root cause remained open |

The diagram at the time was drawn as follows:

```text
Consumer
  |
  v
Release object entry point ----> Current revision in the old record
  |
  v
backend ----> rollout
```

The diagram only expresses the reading order. It does not prove that call relationships existed between the arrows, nor does it prove that `rollout` was the source of the anomaly. The early version described “the comparison landing on rollout” in a way that came close to attribution; this was overstatement. What was actually preserved was a comparison result and a handoff, not a root-cause report.

## Why the “Two States” Affected Rollback

The rollback window depends on the artifact version that was read. When both entry points were simultaneously treated as current, the on-call engineer could not decide which artifact to retain based on only one of them, nor could one green page be treated as evidence that the other had already synchronized. The build queue came from `.github/workflows`, but no complete identifiers were left that could map each queue item to the page revision; therefore, the record preserved only “the same object has two states” and did not turn the gap into a definitive queue failure.

The initial approach was to save both pages, stop further retries, and wait for the user path to recover. This avoided feeding the later final value back into the incident state, but left a practical question: after recovery, could the old entry point still be treated as the current entry point? Materials after version 2 show that this question cannot be answered with screenshots.

## Later Challenges to the Old Conclusion

In APHC-004, the maintenance record required the point in time when the current entry point changed to be marked, and said not to directly subtract the statistics from before and after the two versions. The related supplemental note said that the execution record could be reconstructed, but the explanation for the current result came from an old mirror; version labels were later added to the old mirror, while the provenance chain for the execution record was shown separately.

This did not prove that the old mirror created the two states. It disproved something narrower: the first version assumed that the “current revision” read from the entry point was data of the same kind that could be directly compared. If the explanatory text came from an old mirror while the execution record came from another preservation chain, the two might not belong to the same point in time even if they used the same object name.

APHC-010 subsequently required the current revision and release automation records to be reordered according to the original times, with the page’s final value used only as corroborating evidence. The meaning of “corroborating evidence” here is specific: the final page can show that a value existed later, but it cannot replace the two states already saved at T+00, nor can it replace the missing change time. The early version lacked this distinction, so it misread “consistent later” as “there was no divergence earlier.”

After the old-index cleanup in APHC-007, the execution record could still be opened from the history. This observation also undermined the claim that “the old entry point is no longer valid, so there is no need to look at it.” Whether the old index still exists is not equivalent to whether the historical record is readable; clearing an index and deleting the incident evidence are two different actions.

## Incorrect Attribution Still Retained

The following passage reflects the old wording and is retained for review only, not as a basis for subsequent handling:

> `backend` is normal, which shows that the release automation path has no problems; the recovery of the user path shows that IAM propagation has completed, so the two states are merely display latency.

This statement once made it convenient to close out the shift, but it connected three unverified leaps. The fact that `backend` was normal only shows that the checkpoint displayed no anomaly; recovery of the user path only shows that recovery occurred; and there was no evidence at the time to confirm whether the page discrepancy was display latency. The old-mirror explanation and page-timing issue added later make “merely display latency” even less suitable as the default explanation.

However, we should not conversely conclude that every discrepancy was caused by the mirror. The available materials do not provide the write order of the entry points, a one-to-one mapping between queue items and artifact versions, or a complete record of the request process. We can reject the certainty of the old wording, but we cannot infer a new definitive root cause from that.

## Record Stratification

The original record preserves the initial discrepancy, the `backend` state seen during the shift, and the decision to stop retries. The recovery page preserves the result that the user path recovered. The unconfirmed cause is retained separately to prevent it from being quietly changed into a conclusion after a page update.

This separation is the only part of the incident that became stable. It also explains why seemingly duplicate materials for the same object remain in the knowledge base: one material answers “what was seen at the time,” one answers “whether recovery occurred later,” and another acknowledges “why this happened remains unknown.” They cannot overwrite one another.

## Items Not Completed at the Time

- The sequence of events for the first divergence between the two entry points is still incomplete.
- No preserved record was found that could map the `.github/workflows` queue items, artifact versions, and page revisions to one another individually.
- The change in `apphosting.yaml` in the old record still has no usable explanation; the early version placed it in the same passage as IAM propagation, but they merely appeared at the same time, which does not establish causality.
- After `rollout` was handed off as the comparison direction, no root-cause response was recorded in this record.

Therefore, the historical conclusion retained on this page is: after the anomaly occurred, the user path recovered at T+31; it was initially explained provisionally as IAM propagation. A more reliable reading order for follow-up is to compare the saved time points first, then review the old-mirror explanation, execution record, and final page separately. Do not replace the incident state at T+00 with the revision on the final page, and do not use the normal status of `backend` as a substitute for checking the build queue, artifact version, and rollback window.

The related navigation is retained as APHC-004, APHC-007, and APHC-010; the operations checklist for the exit window is at DOC-40.

# Release Automation Alternative

Deployment automation currently has two comparable handling paths: continue using `service identity`, or split `Web App` out from the existing path. This document retains the latter as a trial proposal and does not treat it as an implementation that has already replaced the former.

The split is not being proposed simply to put the two names in different queues. Existing records show that when the two path segments fail, the rollback exits they go through are different. If they continue to share one processing chain, failures in the build queue will be classified under the same entry point, making artifact versions and rollback windows difficult to assess separately. That difference is the basis for the current preference to split them; it is not enough to show that either side is already more stable.

During the trial, retain the original `service identity` entry point and open a separate `Web App` branch. The branch handles only the build queue formed after the object enters `.github/workflows`, along with the version records for artifacts produced by that queue. The two paths do not take over each other's rollback actions: when a branch needs to be rolled back, handle it first according to that branch's own artifact versions, without also marking the other path's artifacts as unavailable.

This arrangement deliberately leaves caller migration out of scope. Who currently calls `operation poller` has not been verified; until that question is answered, the trial branch should not replace its caller relationship. The project has its own schedule and maintainer, but whether the trial starts and who will integrate it still need to be confirmed separately.

The objection is that splitting out `Web App` will leave two entry points in place, so troubleshooting will first require determining which side received the request. That cost is acceptable only if the build queues and artifact versions can retain separate records instead of collapsing different failure exits into the same result. If they cannot, keeping two entry points adds one more distinction without providing a clearer rollback boundary.

Rollback does not delete the old path or promise to restore any unconfirmed callers. First stop the new branch from entering the queue, retain the version records for artifacts already generated, and then restore the old entry point as the sole handling path. If the caller relationship for `operation poller` is clarified during this period, add it to the decision separately rather than substituting the assumptions in this proposal for it.

To confirm:

- The current callers of `operation poller`;
- Whether the `Web App` branch can retain artifact versions independently;
- Whether any trigger points besides the old entry point need to be restored during rollback.

The original working record is in `docs/adj-deploy/proposals/not-adopted-deploy-release-automation-route.md`.

# Compatibility Directory Failed-Run Procedure

This page handles one failed run of emulator-compatibility-catalog. The goal isn't to fill in the directory, but to preserve the original input and state at the first stopping point so the next shift can continue from there.

## Entry conditions

- Have the original emulator-compatibility-catalog corresponding to this run on hand; don't create another similar input to replace it.
- Open `docs/adj-emulator/runbooks/emulator-compatibility-directory-one-failed-run-on-call-page.md` and first look for records adjacent to this run window.
- If neither the directory nor the records on hand cover this window, leave it empty. Don't directly combine the statistics from the preceding and following segments into one run.

## Proceed to the first failure

1. Start replaying from the original record in the directory; record only the steps that actually occurred.
2. Stop at the first point where progress is impossible. Don't write later guesses, rerun results, or observations from other windows as things that already happened in this run.
3. If the record points to `IAM propagation`, preserve the objects seen at the time and the point where it stopped; don't clean up the state before going back to find the cause.
4. If `Firebase CLI` does not appear, this run ends here. Don't use another entry point in its place, and don't infer from this whether the compatibility directory itself succeeded or failed.

The first failure is not the error that is easiest to explain, but the point in this run where the original input can no longer proceed along the original path. Even when the directory already contains an observation with the same name, use the actual stopping point from this run.

## Stopping actions

After stopping, preserve the original directory entry, outputs already seen, and gaps with no records. If no original record exists, don't backfill a zero result; even an observed zero result must be distinguished from no data collected. The recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment, so don't perform a restore or cleanup on this page.

Write beside the active entry point: the location of the original input, the first failed step, whether `Firebase CLI` appeared, and where gaps remain in the directory. **Who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path?**

If both sides provide only their own partial result, retain the candidate path and do not substitute “entry can be imported” for withdrawal confirmation. It merely prevents a confounded observation from being expanded into an irreversible entry point decision. If the differences are later confirmed to come from product behavior, an entry point adjustment should not replace an assessment on the product side; if they come from cloud resource state, that state should be addressed first; if neither differs but the test environment remains unstable, the window's results still cannot be used as proof for an entry point choice.

The meeting required the actual impact, a coordinator, and an old entry point that can be restored to be documented and retained. These three items cannot be filled in with speculation. What can currently be confirmed is that the differences under discussion hinder people's ability to determine whether the call chain from CLI to API is functioning normally; which usage scenarios are affected cannot yet be confirmed, much less described as a widespread failure of the existing entry point. In the next set of materials, actual impact should be demonstrated by call records under the same conditions, not inferred backward from results within a particular window.

The coordination arrangement is also limited to public entry point maintenance. The maintenance team is responsible for collecting recheck materials and bringing the relevant maintainers into the same review when different entry point arrangements need to be compared. The coordinator should deliver a record that can be reviewed afterward: the same Firebase project, the same region, the initiation point for CLI, and the corresponding API result. A verbal confirmation that “we tried it” cannot replace this record. This arrangement does not change the existing maintenance relationships for the product or cloud resources, nor does it transfer their assessments to the entry point maintenance team.

The recheck sequence is also fixed in this round. First fix the project and region, then initiate a call from CLI and trace it through to the response from API. If the project differs, the target resources may already differ; if the region differs, the resource state may also differ. Unless both conditions are fixed, the entry point choice is not the only change. Only when the call chain under the same conditions is retained can product behavior, target cloud resource state, and test environment noise be examined separately.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Current cli-routing entry point"] --> B["Reproduce in the same project and region"]
  B --> C["Corresponding record from CLI to API"]
  C --> D{"Where does the difference occur"}
  D --> E["Product behavior"]
  D --> F["Target cloud resource state"]
  D --> G["Test environment noise"]
  E --> H["Do not explain it in terms of the change window"]
  F --> H
  G --> H
  H --> I["Retain the old entry point and bring it back for review"]
```

The branches in the diagram are not an automated determination, nor do they call for rerunning every related command and resource. “Complete call” has a very narrow scope here: the record only needs to connect the CLI initiation point with the corresponding API result under the same conditions. If the record stops on the CLI side, it cannot distinguish whether the request failed to arrive, API returned a different result, or subsequent observations were affected by other conditions. If the record contains only the API result, it likewise cannot establish whether the entry point arrangement contributed to the difference.

The product behavior branch is explained by the API result. If API already shows a different product result under the same project and region, public entry point maintenance should not reframe that result as a window issue, much less conceal it by changing the entry point. The target cloud resource state branch requires separately documenting the resource state in the project and region being compared at the time; when resource states differ, the entry point comparison loses its meaning. Test environment noise needs to be retained as a separate phenomenon, rather than lumped under “environment issues” after reproduction fails. At a minimum, it must be possible to tell whether the noise appeared before CLI was initiated, after the API response, or during the observation steps between the two.

Someone proposed reversing the order: establish a change window first, see whether the results change, and then decide whether to continue retaining the old entry point. This approach was not adopted. Once the window goes first, incidental changes in the test environment, the resource state in a particular region, and product responses may all occur at the same time. Even if the results change, an explanatory gap remains: “Was it the window, the resources, or a product change?” The cost of retaining the current entry point is that subsequent decisions will take somewhat longer; the benefit is that the comparison still has a starting point that has not been quietly replaced.

The reversibility associated with the old entry point has two layers. First, until the change window is approved, the current entry point must remain in place and must not first be modified into a form that no longer allows comparison. Second, if a new entry point arrangement is approved later, it must still be possible to restore the arrangement retained in this round. No switching actions or restoration steps are defined in advance here; the specific handoff is handled separately by DOC-52. This decision constrains only the entry point choice: a new arrangement must not irreversibly replace the current baseline.

During a local lookup along the relationship from CLI to API, `src/ensureApiEnabled.ts` and its call name were examined. This location helps with discussing connection points near the entry point, but it cannot substitute for reproducing a run. The public entry point maintenance decision also does not depend on that file becoming the permanent home; the review focuses on whether the differences can be separated along the call chain, not on whether a particular filename looks like the sole entry point.

This round does not predefine a “successful result” for the change window. Specifying in advance that switching is allowed upon seeing a particular response would skip the assessment of whether product behavior and resource state are consistent. The materials brought back to the next review should first include three parts: records from CLI to API under the same conditions, the state of the target cloud resources when the differences were found, and an explanation of whether the test environment has independent noise. If any one of these parts is missing, the entry point arrangement still cannot be assessed as an independent variable.

Three assessments remain unresolved. Whether test environment noise alone is sufficient to cause the current differences has not been confirmed; how the change window would affect the call chain under the same project and region conditions has not been confirmed; no assessment of the scope of actual impact is yet available for reference. These are not incidental to-do items, but direct reasons for not approving a switch in this round. Describing them prematurely as “the entry point is unreliable” or “the window can fix it” would go beyond the available materials.

Therefore, only four decisions are currently in effect: maintain the cli-routing entry point; do not execute the change window; retain the old entry point for restoration and comparison; and have the public entry point maintenance team coordinate the next recheck from CLI to API under the same project and region. No decisions on product conclusions, resource conclusions, test environment attribution, or any switching time were made in this round.

## Assembly Order for the Next Round's Materials

To prevent the next review from again conflating the three types of differences into the single phrase “the entry point is unstable,” assemble the materials in comparison order. The first page identifies only the baseline cli-routing entry point, Firebase project, and region, without assigning a cause in advance. The second page contains the CLI initiation point and the corresponding API result, preserving a verifiable link between them. The third page records the known state of the target cloud resources at the same moment; explicitly leave unknown fields blank rather than inferring them from the response. The fourth page lists test environment noise separately, including the observation step where it appeared and whether it invalidated this comparison.

This sequence is not a new approval process and does not change maintenance responsibilities. It merely allows the review to see which conditions were fixed and which remain unknown. The coordinator is responsible for bringing the materials to the same review and confirming that the comparison still uses the restorable old entry point as its baseline; the coordinator does not explain the results on behalf of product or resource maintainers. If the project, region, or entry point changes midway, these materials serve only as a record of one run and cannot support a switching decision.

Perform three checks first during the review. First, whether CLI and API come from the same project and region; if they cannot be matched, stop the entry point comparison. Second, whether the target resource state has been recorded separately; if not, leave the matter unresolved and do not attribute the differences to product behavior. Third, whether test environment noise is sufficient to invalidate the observations; if so, record where the noise occurred and repeat the call under the same conditions, rather than describing an incidental result as a benefit of the window. Only after all three checks can be answered should there be discussion of whether the change window warrants a separate, reversible comparison.

Continue to retain two columns on the final page of the materials: approved and not approved. The approved items remain limited to maintaining the current entry point, retaining the restoration baseline, and organizing a recheck under the same conditions; the unapproved items remain switching directly, using window results in place of causal attribution, and declaring the entry point failed without knowing the scope of impact. If new evidence emerges later, append the date and reasons beside these two columns rather than rewriting this round's decision, so that later readers can see how the conclusions changed.

## Boundaries of the Reversibility Conditions

In this record, “reversible” constrains only the entry point arrangement; it does not promise that product state or cloud resource state can be rolled back. Any future experiment must first save identifying information for the current entry point and specify in the review materials which baseline will be restored. If the baseline cannot be clearly identified, the change window does not enter execution discussions. This boundary also prevents a one-time improvement in the test environment from being mistakenly recorded as grounds for a permanent switch. The unresolved items remain for the next recheck under the same conditions.

# Shared Entry Point Switch Handoff Process

Handoffs for maintaining a shared entry point can become distorted at the last step: the person performing the switch sees that the task is finished, while the person taking over receives only a section of log and does not know which consumers have already left the old entry point. This lays out the handoff materials in switch order. The focus is not on adding a separate explanation for every secrets call, but on making the old entry point, candidate path, and rollback action line up in the same record.

The lookup for the entry point location is documented separately in DOC-53. This page only covers what should be left behind when consumers move from the old entry point to the candidate path, and when the status should still be written as migration in progress.

## Determining Whether the Handoff Is Complete

A switch must be able to answer at least three questions.

First, who the known consumers are and which ones are still using the old entry point. Here, "known" includes only consumers of secrets that have already been counted; callers that were not found cannot be considered migrated just because the trial run succeeded. Each row in the list should retain the consumer name, current entry point, path to be used, and whether it can roll back independently. When a consumer has no name, do not merge it into one row as "other callers."

Second, whether the candidate path has actually been used by a consumer that can roll back independently. This consumer is not a stand-in for full migration, but a small-scope switch record: it can return to the old entry point without waiting for another group to modify the shared entry point before it can recover. The rollback capability must be written down before the trial run; do not wait until the candidate path has a problem to guess whether the old entry point is still usable.

Third, whether the handoff package allows another person to reconstruct this operation. If any of the command parameters, request body, long-running task name, or terminal-state object is missing, it only shows that someone performed an action; it does not show that the person taking over can determine which step the action is at. The final log can serve as supporting evidence, but cannot replace the terminal-state object; logs often retain only the last sentence and do not preserve the old entry point, request content, or the object corresponding to the task.

If any one of these three questions is unanswered, the page status remains "migration in progress." This does not prevent a trial run; it avoids writing the partial result of the candidate path as if the shared entry point had already completed its switch.

## Retained from the Initial Draft: The Earlier Wrap-Up Approach

The initial draft made the process very short: count the consumers of secrets, choose one consumer that can roll back, run it through the candidate path, and hand off after success. This sequence still works, but the word "success" is too broad.

The earlier approach left at that time was:

```text
Old entry point -> Choose one consumer -> Candidate path -> Final log
```

This line did not identify the request body or explain how the long-running task name and terminal-state object belonged to the same trial run. More problematically, the earlier approach would lead the person taking over to treat the final log as the completion signal, with no place to record compatible callers that were still using the old entry point. This section is retained to show that the fields added later address a handoff gap rather than overturning the original trial-run sequence.

## Establish a Consumer Ledger First

Before starting the switch, the maintainer should create the following record for the known consumers. The fields do not need to be written as a project-level ledger; one trial run per row is sufficient. Leave cells without actual values blank; do not substitute example values.

| Consumer | Old entry point | Candidate path | Can roll back independently | Current record |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Known consumer | Entry point used before the switch | Path used for this trial run | Where to return during rollback | Not started, in progress, or archived |

Write the actual entry point under "old entry point," not a generic term such as "default method." The candidate path should also be listed alongside the old entry point, so that someone does not later see only the new shared entry point name and fail to find the place that needs to be restored.

When counting consumers, first distinguish between two types of records. The first type is callers whose use of secrets has been confirmed; they enter this handoff ledger. The second type is compatible consumers that have been mentioned but whose use has not yet been confirmed; they must not be quietly included in the migrated count and should be listed separately after the ledger as uncovered callers. This makes it possible to state accurately after the trial run which type is covered, rather than giving a seemingly complete total.

Do not count the same consumer multiple times just because it has multiple logs. The handoff is concerned with whether it still depends on the old entry point and whether it has an independent rollback action. Multiple log fragments can only be attached to the record in the same row.

## Trial the Candidate Path

Before the trial run, select a consumer from the ledger that can roll back independently. The reason for the selection must be specific to this consumer: its old entry point is still usable, it can recover independently after the switch, and its operation record can be stored separately from those of other consumers. A consumer without a rollback action, Fang Ke, can remain in a later batch, but is not suitable as the first trial subject.

Complete the trial-run record in the order the events occur:

1. Write down the old entry point used by the consumer before the switch and the candidate path to be adopted.
2. Save the actual command parameters. The parameters must come from that operation; do not treat a command copied from elsewhere as the record for this operation.
3. Save the actual request body. Keep the request body and command parameters in the same trial-run record to avoid finding only half of them later.
4. Save the long-running task name. If the operation produces a long-running task, the name should correspond to this request; do not leave only a description saying "the task completed."
5. Save the terminal-state object. The terminal-state object is used to determine what state this candidate path ultimately produced; it is more suitable than the final log for judging the handoff.
6. Write down the rollback action and the old entry point after rollback. If the rollback action has not been recorded, do not mark this consumer as able to roll back independently.

If the candidate path does not produce an identifiable terminal-state object during the trial run, stop at that item; do not use the log to fill in the judgment. If the long-running task name is missing, return to the operation record and look for it instead of filling it in from memory. The fields in the handoff package must come from the same switch; combining the request body from one request with the task name from another will cause later readers to misjudge whether the problem is with the shared entry point or with the record itself.

After the trial run, the record should read as one continuous chain: which consumer left which old entry point, which candidate path it used, which parameters and request body it used, which long-running task it produced, and which terminal-state object it ended with; if recovery is needed, what should be done. This is more suitable for a handoff than attaching multiple screenshots, because screenshots usually cannot show whether they belong to the same operation.

## Expand from the Trial Run to the Remaining Consumers

After the candidate path has been trialed, do not immediately mark all known consumers as migrated. First mark the trial consumer separately in the ledger, and keep the others separated by old entry point and compatibility status.

Subsequent switches can be performed in small batches. Each batch should include only consumers already listed in the ledger, and should retain its own command parameters, request body, long-running task name, and terminal-state object. Do not share one "completed" conclusion between batches: the terminal-state object for one batch can only describe the consumers involved in that batch.

Compatible callers are the part most likely to be missed in a handoff. Even if they do not enter the candidate path for now, they should remain on the uncovered list, with the old entry point they still depend on documented. After the candidate-path records are complete, decide whether to include them in the next batch; until then, the old entry point remains a path that must be maintained.

Maintaining the old entry point does not mean continuing to add new consumers. During the switch, its purpose is to provide known callers with a recovery location and give the trial run's rollback action a real destination. If the maintainer removes the old entry point prematurely, subsequent rollback records lose their meaning, and the person taking over cannot distinguish a problem with the candidate path from a problem with the recovery path.

## How to Arrange the Handoff Package

Archive handoff materials by switch rather than scattering them by material type. The recommended reading order is:

```text
Consumer
  ├─ Old entry point before the switch
  ├─ Candidate path
  ├─ Command parameters
  ├─ Request body
  ├─ Long-running task name
  ├─ Terminal-state object
  └─ Rollback action and old entry point after recovery
```

The "terminal-state object" here is the primary record for judging the handoff; attach the final log only beside that object. If someone can provide only a log, leave the item in progress and hand it off only after the correspondence between the task and object can be restored.

When taking over, look at the consumer ledger first, then open each trial-run record. Do not work backward from a pile of tasks or logs to guess which consumers have been switched. The three statuses—migrated, in progress, and uncovered—should coexist in the ledger: they reflect facts about different consumers, not an unfinished document.

## Rollback and Retaining the Old Entry Point

The rollback action is responsible only for consumers that actually went through the trial run. When recording a rollback, it must be possible to see which old entry point it returns to from the candidate path, and whether the consumer remains in the ledger after returning to the old entry point. An operation without a separate recovery location should not be written as "can roll back independently."

If the candidate-path record is missing the request body, long-running task name, or terminal-state object, prioritize stopping the expansion of the migration scope. The old entry point that already exists can remain in place, and the missing fields can be marked under the corresponding consumer; do not delete the old path just to make the batch look complete.

When the old entry point can be taken offline depends on whether the known consumers and uncovered callers all have clear destinations. As long as the uncovered list still contains callers that depend on the old entry point, or any migrated record cannot be used to reconstruct its rollback action, the handoff should not describe the old entry point as removable.

## Addendum After This Review

The key addition from the review was not more logs, but downgrading the "final log" from the basis for completion to supporting material. The command parameters, request body, long-running task name, and terminal-state object that were not explicitly written in the initial draft are now parts that must be handed off with the record for every trial run.

Compatible callers that remain unconfirmed continue to be listed separately. They do not automatically acquire migration status just because the candidate path has been trialed. When the handoff for the shared entry point switch ends here, the person taking over should be able to continue maintaining the old entry point, recheck the candidate path, or perform the recorded rollback action for any one listed consumer.
